summary: A snapshot of the standardization status of Internet protocols as tracked by the IETF at the time. It served as a reference list of which protocols were at which maturity level. Its status is historic, and it was replaced by RFC 2800.

eli5.summary: It is a class report card listing how far along each Internet rule has come. A newer card has since replaced it.

questions: what is the internet official protocol standards list
where to find status of internet standards in 2000
how does the ietf standardization process work
subtitle: The IETF's snapshot of which protocols were standards in 2000.

tldr.problem: The Internet has hundreds of specifications (RFCs). Engineers and operators need to know which protocols are official standards, which are still being tested, which are historical, and what maturity level each has reached.
tldr.mechanism: This document lists every protocol the IETF considers an official Internet Standard, plus those in earlier stages of standardization (Draft Standard, Proposed Standard, Experimental) and those that are Historic. It organizes them by maturity level and provides both RFC number and standard number (STD) references.
tldr.outcome: This was a periodic snapshot of the standardization landscape. As new protocols matured and old ones were replaced, later editions were published (RFC 2800, then RFC 2900). It served as a reference point in time for what the Internet standards process had produced.

today: RFC 2700 is Historic. It was replaced by RFC 2800 in May 2001, which was in turn replaced by RFC 2900 in August 2001. The Internet standards process has continued to evolve, and the IETF no longer publishes periodic snapshots of this form; current standards information is maintained online.

sections.title: What this document is
sections.content:
RFC 2700 is a standards status document published by the IETF in August 2000. It describes the state of standardization of protocols used in the Internet, categorizing each protocol by its maturity level within the standardization process. The document is not a complete index of all RFCs; it lists only those protocols that have gone through (or are going through) the formal IETF standardization process.

The IETF publishes updated versions of this document periodically as protocols advance through the standardization stages.
sections.eli5: This is the IETF's official list of Internet protocols, organized by how official and tested each one is. When new rules are adopted or old ones retire, the IETF publishes an updated list.

sections.title: How the standardization process works
sections.content:
The IETF uses a multi-stage process to standardize protocols. When the IETF publishes a new technical specification as an RFC, it starts as a Proposed Standard and must demonstrate widespread interest and engineering consensus. Once it passes review and two independent interoperable implementations exist, it moves to Draft Standard. After additional operational experience, it can become an Internet Standard (the highest level).

The document also lists Experimental RFCs, which are protocols for research or testing that are not on a path to standardization, and Historic RFCs, which are protocols that are no longer used or have been superseded.
sections.eli5: Protocols start as test rules, move to trial status, and eventually become official standards if they work well. If a rule stops being useful, it gets marked as old history.

sections.title: The lists
sections.content:
This document provides lists of protocols organized by standardization level. Standard Protocols are listed both by STD number (a stable reference that persists even if the RFC is updated) and by RFC number. Each entry shows the protocol name, title, RFC number, and STD number (if assigned). Draft Standard and Proposed Standard sections list hundreds of protocols in various stages of development. Experimental and Historic sections list protocols that are not on a path to official standardization.

Asterisks mark protocols that changed status since the previous edition of this document, making it easy to spot what has moved between maturity levels.
sections.eli5: The document is organized like a filing system: official standards here, rules being tested there, old retired rules in another place. Little stars show what moved since the last time the document was published.

sections.title: Why it matters
sections.content:
This document served as a critical reference for anyone deploying or understanding Internet protocols. When RFC 2700 was published in August 2000, it reflected the consensus of the Internet community on what was ready for production use (Standards), what was nearly ready (Draft Standards), what was promising (Proposed Standards), and what was experimental or obsolete.

Because protocols and standardization status change over time, the IETF publishes a new edition when significant changes have accumulated. This edition was replaced by RFC 2800 in May 2001.
sections.eli5: This list was like a snapshot in time: it told you exactly which protocols were official and trusted on that particular date in 2000. When enough new protocols were adopted, a new edition came out with the updated list.
